{"id": "11:114/q14", "question": "Which sins are removed, and on what conditions?", "turns_on": "How to read the condition about major sins and the scope of divine expiation.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q14/p1", "position": "Minor sins are expiated if major sins are avoided.", "reasons": "The prayer report conditions expiation on avoiding majors. Ibn Ashur cites 53:32 and 4:31. Sunni majority make avoidance a condition of the whole promise, while another group treats majors as excluded from what is erased; Alusi prefers that distinction and argues prayers erase minors even when majors exist. Al-Damghani gives minor sins as a sense of sayyi'at that good deeds remove and cites 46:16 for overlooking them."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p2", "position": "Minor sins require repentance and nonpersistence for erasure.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya invokes sins falling with ablution water and expert legal theorists; Abu Hayyan concurs. Alusi records disagreement and stresses that expiation does not end the duty to repent."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p3", "position": "Repentance can expiate major sins.", "reasons": "Jishumi favors Abu Ali's reading; Tabrisi says punishment is cancelled by repentance without dispute. Al-Subki reports debate over whether forgiveness after repentance for sins is certain or presumed."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p4", "position": "Some good deeds can expiate major as well as minor sins.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq says a later good deed can remove a forgotten grave sin. Al-Dhakha'ir cites promises of forgiveness of past and future sins; Ibn al-Mundhir inclines to this. Alusi answers critics who invoke Murji'ism by retaining the duty of repentance."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p5", "position": "Faith erases unbelief and at least removes eternal punishment, so believers' sins cannot ultimately harm them.", "reasons": "Razi reports this argument by its proponents."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p6", "position": "A major sin may be lightened when an expiatory act finds no minor sins.", "reasons": "Al-Nawawi presents this as a hope."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p7", "position": "Avoidance of major sins can itself expiate minor sins at each time, when restraint is intentional.", "reasons": "Al-Balqini reads 4:31 over a lifetime; Alusi rejects that reading with al-Qadi and Ghazali. Ghazali requires ability and desire to commit the major sin."}, {"id": "11:114/q14/p8", "position": "Punishment for minor sins remains possible despite avoidance of majors.", "reasons": "Alusi reports Sunni authorities citing 4:48 and 18:49; Mu'tazila deny this from 4:31, which may concern unbelief."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q15", "question": "What happened in the incident linked to this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports describe new revelation or application of an existing verse, and the varying details of the man's act and remedy.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q15/p1", "position": "A man had illicit physical contact with a woman short of intercourse, confessed, and the Prophet applied the verse and prayer as expiation.", "reasons": "Accounts vary: a date seller lured a woman home, a man kissed or touched her backside, or a woman by a pool occasioned temptation. Some say the Prophet waited until revelation; others say Gabriel brought it after Asr. Abu Bakr and Umar advised concealment and repentance. Some reports prescribe thorough ablution and two units, others prayer with the Prophet. Tirmidhi grades Ibn Masud's reports hasan sahih, Abu al-Yusr's hasan gharib with a weak transmitter; Ibn Ashur says Muadh and Abu al-Yusr routes are weak. Ibn Abi Hatim and Durr preserve other versions. Al-Burhan reports a date seller who tried to seduce a buyer; its Ibn Mas'ud report in both Sahihs describes a kiss followed by the Prophet's application of this verse."}, {"id": "11:114/q15/p2", "position": "The pool encounter ended in remorse, with forgiveness sought and four prayer units prescribed.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir calls Yahya ibn Ja'da's account mursal. The reports differ on whether the man found a woman by a pool or approached her while she bathed, and whether impotence stopped him."}, {"id": "11:114/q15/p3", "position": "The verse already existed, and the Prophet applied its general rule to the penitent.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites a Tirmidhi transmission saying the Prophet recited the verse without saying it newly descended; 'revealed' can mean applied to the case."}, {"id": "11:114/q15/p4", "position": "The verse was newly revealed in response to the confession.", "reasons": "The Prophet's silence or delay until revelation is a recurrent detail; Ibn Ashur notes this wording would make the verse Medinan."}, {"id": "11:114/q15/p5", "position": "The verse descended again when a new incident arose, recalling its existing ruling.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says an already revealed verse may recur when a new case prompts it; this explains a report of revelation without requiring the first descent then."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q16", "question": "Who was the man in the confession report?", "turns_on": "Variant transmission of the man's name, kunya, and tribe.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q16/p1", "position": "Abu al-Yusr, the Ansari date seller; names given include Amr ibn Ghaziya and Ka'b ibn Amr.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir preserve divergent personal names for Abu al-Yusr. {"id": "11:114/q17", "question": "To whom did the Prophet say the verse's remedy applies?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q17/p1", "position": "It applies generally to all believers or the Prophet's community who act on it.", "reasons": "The questioner is variously Umar, Muadh, or Abu al-Yusr (Ibn al-Jawzi). {"id": "11:114/q18", "question": "What legal consequence follows for an unlawful kiss or touch?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q18/p1", "position": "It does not incur the fixed penalty for intercourse.", "reasons": "Qurtubi infers this from the incident and expiation through prayer."}, {"id": "11:114/q18/p2", "position": "Even a man and woman found in one garment incur neither a fixed penalty nor discretionary punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Mundhir is reported to choose this on the basis of the incident."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q19", "question": "What is the grammatical form of ذكرى?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q19/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun ending in feminine alif, with other attested forms and a plural.", "reasons": "Abu Ali compares العدوى, الدعوى and شورى; Sibawayh records الذكر with dal and cites Ibn Muqbil's line, alongside 12:45. {"id": "11:114/q20", "question": "To what does ذلك point?", "turns_on": "Which antecedent the demonstrative resumes.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q20/p1", "position": "The preceding counsel and commands, including steadfastness and prayer.", "reasons": "Kashshaf starts at the uprightness command; Tabari includes this surah's commands and prohibitions. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi mention avoiding transgression and unjust rulers; Biqai includes warning and consolation."}, {"id": "11:114/q20/p2", "position": "The command to establish prayer at these times.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan prefers the nearest antecedent; Ibn Atiyya says prayer supplies a cause and setting for remembrance."}, {"id": "11:114/q20/p3", "position": "The statement or promise that good deeds erase sins.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says this encourages good deeds; Jishumi calls it the promise itself."}, {"id": "11:114/q20/p4", "position": "The Qur'an.", "reasons": "Wahidi says it is an admonition for one who remembers the Quran."}, {"id": "11:114/q20/p5", "position": "This, meaning the present admonition.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas takes ذلك in the sense of هذا."}]}

{"id": "11:114/q22", "question": "How does the verse connect to nearby commands and other verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q22/p1", "position": "Prayer follows the command to remain upright as the foremost aid to steadfastness, and its expiatory power explains the command.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says 'indeed' emphasizes the causal explanation and links 29:45; Biqai says prayer cures the weakness behind lesser sins."}, {"id": "11:114/q22/p2", "position": "Other verses supply or parallel these prayer times.", "reasons": "Muqatil recalls Moses' prayer for remembrance at 20:14; Hasan invokes 17:78; Razi and Elmalili cite 20:130; Bursevi adds 50:39–40. {"id": "11:114/q23", "question": "Was this verse revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Whether 'revealed' in the confession account denotes first revelation or application of an earlier verse.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q23/p1", "position": "It was revealed in Medina as an exception within the surah.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Qatada infer this from the confession report's 'revealed to him' wording; many commentators list verses 12, 17 and 114 as possible exceptions. Al-Itqan lists this verse among three Medinan exceptions in Hud and supports its dating with several sound routes about Abu al-Yusr."}, {"id": "11:114/q23/p2", "position": "It is Meccan along with the whole surah; the Prophet later applied it to the penitent.", "reasons": "Rashid Rida rejects Medina dating as unconvincing. Ibn Kathir suggests it may predate the five prayers of the Night Journey, when two daily prayers and night vigil were required."}, {"id": "11:114/q23/p3", "position": "If newly revealed in Medina, it was placed here for coherence with steadfastness and patience.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur points to the adjacent commands at 11:112 and 11:115."}, {"id": "11:114/q23/p4", "position": "It descended twice, first in Mecca and then in Medina.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan and al-Zarkashi in al-Itqan use repeated descent to reconcile the Meccan status of Hud with the Medinan confession report; recurrence magnifies and renews a verse."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q24", "question": "What distinct reports illustrate the verse's hope and expiation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q24/p1", "position": "The five prayers wash away sins like repeated bathing in a river or leaves falling from a branch.", "reasons": "Salman shakes a dry branch; the Prophet's river image asks whether dirt could remain after five baths. Abu Dharr's report in al-Itqan identifies the testimony of unity as the best good deed."}, {"id": "11:114/q24/p8", "position": "Every deed is recorded, so one should not belittle a sin or a good deed.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq warns of angels recording public and hidden acts."}, {"id": "11:114/q24/p9", "position": "A later good deed swiftly overtakes an old sin.", "reasons": "Al-Itqan transmits this image from a weak Ibn Abbas report attributed to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q25", "question": "What inward reading does the verse support?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q25/p1", "position": "Prayer and remembrance bring light that clears sensory darkness and sustains presence.", "reasons": "Qashani relates five prayers to five senses and night vigil to refining natural powers; Bursevi describes the luminous spirit nourished by good works, and Wasiti contrasts obedience's light with sin's darkness. {"id": "11:114/q26", "question": "What senses can al-sayyi'at have in Quranic usage?", "turns_on": "The word's sense changes with its Quranic context; these parallels do not all interpret its occurrence here.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q26/p1", "position": "Bad deeds, the opposite of good deeds.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives the basic contrast."}, {"id": "11:114/q26/p2", "position": "Associating partners with God.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this Quranic use at 4:18 and 10:27."}, {"id": "11:114/q26/p3", "position": "Punishment or the consequences of wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this use at 39:51."}, {"id": "11:114/q26/p4", "position": "Harm or misfortune.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites afflictions in 7:168 and 11:10."}, {"id": "11:114/q26/p5", "position": "Evil or wicked schemes.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this sense at 40:45."}, {"id": "11:114/q26/p6", "position": "Men having sex with men.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this use in the account of Lot's people at 11:78."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q27", "question": "How is the ta in الصلاة طرفي pronounced in large assimilation?", "turns_on": "The exceptional transmission from al-Susi versus other performance authorities.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q27/p1", "position": "The ta assimilates into the following emphatic ta.", "reasons": "Al-Itqan lists this exact phrase; Ibn al-Jazari reports that most performance authorities favor assimilation for homorganicity and the strength of the following consonant."}, {"id": "11:114/q27/p2", "position": "Al-Susi clearly articulates the ta in one reported route.", "reasons": "Ibn Habash alone reports this from al-Susi, citing the light vowel and preceding still consonant; Ibn al-Jazari notes other authorities' assimilation."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q28", "question": "What large assimilation is cited at السيئات ذلك?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q28/p1", "position": "The final ta is assimilated before dhal.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari lists this exact join among nine instances of assimilation before dhal."}]}

{"id": "11:21/q03", "question": "What does 'went astray from them' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ḍalla stresses disappearance and failure to help or the separation of worshippers from supposed partners onto different paths.", "positions": [{"id": "11:21/q03/p1", "position": "Their inventions disappeared or were lost, providing none of the help or benefit they had expected.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says ḍalla means lost or perished and not found where hoped. Al-Ṭabarī says supposed deities were only stone, wood, or copper, and no longer accompany worshippers. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ḥasan, al-Baghawī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, and others describe failed hopes of benefit or intercession. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says their imaginary inventions vanish when worldly life ends and truth appears. Ibn Kathīr adds that idols harm rather than help and disown their worshippers, citing 46:6, 19:81–82, 29:25, and 2:166. The Study Quran says the fabrications forsake them, mentioning 6:24, 6:54, 10:30, 16:87, and 28:75. Al-Ṭabarī also mentions 6:24."}, {"id": "11:21/q03/p2", "position": "Their alleged partners part company with them and take a different path.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says the worshippers head to Hell, while a supposed deity that is God's ally may instead head to Paradise; their paths do not coincide."}]}
{"id": "11:21/q04", "question": "When do the inventions go astray from them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:21/q04/p1", "position": "At the Resurrection or in the afterlife, when worldly life has ended.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, specifies the Day of Resurrection. {"id": "11:21/q05", "question": "What are the things they had fabricated?", "turns_on": "Whether the fabrication names supposed deities, lies and beliefs, imagined intercession, association of partners, or wider deceptive powers and half-truths; Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's lies and Qatāda's association of partners separately.", "positions": [{"id": "11:21/q05/p1", "position": "Their supposed gods, idols, or divine partners.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ḥasan speak of fabricated gods or hoped-for idols. Asad adds deceptive half-truths and mentions 6:112; The Study Quran includes ideas and religious beliefs."}, {"id": "11:21/q05/p3", "position": "The intercession they imagined from angels, idols, or supposed intercessors.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī specifies invented intercession for angels and idols; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī also mention hoped-for or imagined intercession."}, {"id": "11:21/q05/p4", "position": "Their association of partners with God.", "reasons": "Qatāda, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, gives this as an alternative to Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation in terms of worldly lies."}, {"id": "11:21/q05/p5", "position": "False powers and deceptive half-truths such as luck, wealth, personal power, nationalism, and materialism.", "reasons": "Asad says these obscure spiritual values and waste people's lives; he mentions 6:112."}]}
{"id": "11:21/q06", "question": "How does the surrounding description bear on the loss announced here?", "turns_on": "The notes supply distinct explanations of the surrounding passage rather than competing readings of one expression.", "positions": [{"id": "11:21/q06/p1", "position": "The description of the unjust forger shows that ignorance of God can lead to lying about Him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says this answers those who supposed that ignorance of God would do no harm, since none is more unjust than one who lies about Him."}, {"id": "11:21/q06/p2", "position": "A poetic gloss describes culpable action as what the hands earned or committed.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports a poetic example for the surrounding verb jarama, glossing it as what the hands earned or committed."}, {"id": "11:21/q06/p3", "position": "The surrounding terms describe inability to prevent God's will, multiplied punishment, and bodily capacity.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī defines inability to thwart as inability to prevent what God wills, doubling as increase by an equal or larger amount, and capacity as a power by which limbs act."}]}
{"id": "11:22/q01", "question": "What does لا جرم assert here?", "turns_on": "Whether la jarama is treated as a fixed assertion of certainty, a rebuttal followed by a verb of earning or becoming true, a negation of cutting or prevention, or a negation of doubt; the cited poetry's case and sense are disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q01/p1", "position": "It affirms as certain or true that they are the greatest losers; the idiom can also convey inevitability, absence of doubt, or oath-like emphasis.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Abbas as reported by Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, and other exegetes gloss it 'indeed' or 'truly'; al-Baghawi also gives 'rather indeed' and al-Farra's 'without doubt.' Al-Tabari calls it an idiom of certainty associated literally with earning sin and inevitability. Al-Farra, reported by al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and al-Tabataba'i, derives the familiar emphatic use from 'no escape' or 'inevitably' through frequent use and notes its oath-like force; al-Sirafi's report in al-Alusi similarly traces an older sense of keeping someone from sin. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Farra, Muhammad ibn Yazid and others transmit the 'truly' account in al-Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin. Al-Tabrisi reports the decisive-assertion sense; al-Baydawi says no one is more manifestly a loser. Ibn Ashur calls it a certainty idiom, treating jarama as a fossilized noun for inevitability or no alternative. Al-Biqa'i says denying the contrary establishes the assertion, comparing the emphatic force of la to innama; he reports al-Farahi's derivation from cutting and its oath-like use. Al-Nasafi and al-Alusi report the compound or conventional certainty sense."}, {"id": "11:22/q01/p2", "position": "The negation rebuts a supposed benefit, while jarama says their deed or unbelief earned the loss or punishment that follows.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq in al-Nahhas and al-Zajjaj in al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Samin, al-Biqa'i and al-Alusi read la as rejecting expected benefit, especially from idols; Ibn al-Anbari specifies the unbelievers' hope that punishment will be diverted. {"id": "11:22/q02", "question": "How are لا جرم and the following أن clause constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is compounded, a rebuttal followed by a past verb, or a negated noun; these analyses assign different cases and syntactic roles to the following an clause.", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q02/p1", "position": "La jarama is a fixed compound of negation and jarama meaning 'certainly'; the following an clause is nominative, as its subject.", "reasons": "Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Farra and Muhammad ibn Yazid are reported by al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi; al-Khalil says la responds to prior speech rather than opening a statement. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi transmit al-Khalil and Sibawayh's compound analysis. Al-Samin compares its fixed form with khamsata ashar and cites 16:62. Al-Nasafi reports the compound analysis. Ibn Atiyya contrasts Sibawayh's nominative an with al-Zajjaj's accusative one. Al-Biqa'i reports a related compound-past-verb account from Sibawayh and al-Khalil."}, {"id": "11:22/q02/p2", "position": "La rebuts a preceding claim; jarama is a past verb meaning 'earned,' with an implicit doer and the following an clause as its accusative object.", "reasons": "Abu Ishaq and al-Zajjaj in al-Nahhas, al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, al-Samin, al-Biqa'i and al-Alusi reject the supposed benefit and give the deed or unbelief as jarama's omitted subject. Ibn al-Anbari specifies an implicit subject referring to disbelief; al-Samin gives the deeds as subject and cites 75:1 and 4:65 for reply-like la. Abu Hayyan notes that al-Zajjaj rejects compounding and cites poetry for the earning verb. Al-Razi and al-Tabrisi explain the same rebuttal and earned loss. Al-Nasafi gives the claim as what earns the loss. Al-Alusi supplies an omitted clause such as 'their deed benefits them' and an unnamed poet for the verbal sense."}, {"id": "11:22/q02/p3", "position": "La negates jarama as a noun of cutting or prevention; the an clause is its predicate or depends on an omitted preposition.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports the negation-plus-cutting analysis. Al-Kisa'i, as reported by al-Alusi, treats jarama as la's indeclinable noun, with omitted predicate and omitted preposition before an, yielding no opposition or prevention; al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi record his no-prevention interpretation."}, {"id": "11:22/q02/p4", "position": "La is an extra emphatic particle, leaving the assertion or earned outcome to follow.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi reports extra la for the emphatic 'truly'; al-Wahidi reports an extra-la analysis in which their deed earns regret. Al-Biqa'i reports al-Radi and al-Saqafsi allowing extra la because the phrase bears oath force."}, {"id": "11:22/q02/p5", "position": "La negates a genus and jarama is its accusative noun; the pair is the subject and the following an clause its predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Samin gives this analysis, with the sense 'certainly.' Al-Kisa'i's analysis as reported by al-Alusi also omits a preposition before an; Ibn Ashur's fossilized-noun account likewise makes an depend on an omitted preposition."}, {"id": "11:22/q02/p7", "position": "La is negative and jarama is the verb 'became true'; the following clause functions as its subject.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this from Sibawayh and explains that the unbelievers' expected benefit fails because loss is certain. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi report Sibawayh and al-Akhfash with la as reply and jarama as 'deserved/was certain'; al-Wahidi records al-Farra and Abu al-Abbas objecting to their poetic proof because Ghatafan is accusative."}, {"id": "11:22/q02/p8", "position": "La jarama is a fossilized noun of inevitability, with an governed by an omitted preposition.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives this construction and notes that the expression can introduce an oath-like assertion. {"id": "11:22/q03", "question": "What forms of لا جرم are reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q03/p1", "position": "The expression has dialectal and transmitted variants in particles, vowels, and omission of final mīm.", "reasons": "Al-Kisa'i as reported by al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi lists la jarama, la an dha jarama and la an/dha-related forms, including a Fazara form without mim. Al-Farra adds Banu Amir's la dha jarama and a damma on jim. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi list la dha jarama, la an dha jarama, la an dha or la an/dha jarama, and la jar, explaining shortened la jar by frequent use. Al-Samin records different vowels, dha- and in-initial forms, and Abu Amr's la jar and a changed-rhyme form; Abu Amr likens dropped mim to shortened sawfa. Abu Hayyan notes the variants transmitted by al-Nahhas and al-Farra. Al-Alusi says inserted particles are generally extra, tentatively treats a form lacking la as needing no further assertion, and notes that lexicographers doubt the eloquent-Arabic status of some forms. Al-Biqa'i distinguishes fath from kasra through original no-alternative and later oath-like senses."}]}
{"id": "11:22/q04", "question": "Who are 'they' in this judgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q04/p1", "position": "The disbelievers just described, including those who denied the afterlife and relied on fabricated objects of worship.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies them as these unbelievers. {"id": "11:22/q05", "question": "What comparison does 'in the afterlife, the greatest losers' imply?", "turns_on": "Whether the superlative compares them with other afterlife inhabitants or compares their enduring afterlife loss with their worldly loss; al-Tabataba'i favors the first from the verse's apparent restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q05/p1", "position": "Among the inhabitants of the afterlife, they are the most ruined, with no prospect of salvation while they persist in defiance.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i treats the superlative as comparing them with other people there and invokes 6:12, 36:9-10 and 45:23. He prefers this reading because the verse appears to restrict the greatest losers to them in the afterlife. Al-Baghawi says all are losers but these are the greatest; al-Baydawi says no one is more plainly or greatly a loser there. Al-Alusi reads degree or amount, and Ibn Ashur says they combine forms of misery dispersed among deluded nations. Al-Samarrai contrasts these greatest losers with the losers of 16:107-108: the former also obstructed God's path and misled others, bringing multiplied punishment, while the latter preferred worldly life without that added harm to others."}, {"id": "11:22/q05/p2", "position": "Their afterlife loss exceeds their loss in this brief worldly life, since the former lasts forever; they lose both lives.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports this as another possible comparison and cites 46:35, while preferring the comparison with afterlife inhabitants. Al-Razi says the worldly object chosen over faith perishes; Abu Hayyan distinguishes their endless loss from sinners whose punishment ends. Al-Tabataba'i also says deeds intensify through their afterlife consequences, citing 17:72; Ibn Ashur says they lose this world and the next."}]}

{"id": "11:22/q07", "question": "Why are they called the greatest losers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q07/p1", "position": "Their rejection brings the fullest, enduring loss and punishment in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says they exchanged their Paradise homes for the homes of Paradise's people in Hell. Ibn Kathir expands the exchange: Paradise's heights and delights for Hell's depths and punishments, and God's nearness and vision for anger. Al-Razi says the worldly thing chosen instead of noble faith cannot last. Al-Nasafi says they themselves turned away and led others astray. Abu Hayyan contrasts their endless loss with sinners' finite punishment and eventual relief. Ibn Ashur calls loss a trader metaphor: they expected gain and suffered harm; he says they combine punishments scattered across deluded peoples and suffer misery precisely where they expected joy, losing both worlds, citing 18:103-104. Al-Tabataba'i says disbelief destroys themselves with no salvation while defiance persists, and reports that their afterlife loss exceeds worldly loss because it lasts forever; he adds that deeds intensify through their afterlife consequences, citing 17:72. Al-Alusi says greatest can indicate degree or amount, while an alternative cutting analysis makes their loss uninterrupted. Al-Baghawi observes that others also lose, but these lose most. Muqatil, al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i affirm the superlative. Islahi traces their ruin to capacities squandered on false worship and the failure of imagined divine supports. Al-Samarrai says they obstructed God's path and misled others, so their punishment was multiplied; he contrasts them with the people of 16:107-108, who preferred worldly life but did not add that harm to others."}]}
{"id": "11:22/q08", "question": "How does this judgment sum up the preceding account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:22/q08/p1", "position": "It concludes the account of their rejected guidance, false worship, failed claims, and inability to avert punishment by naming their final loss.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the final sentence sums up their exposure, punishment, refusal to hear warnings and neglect of evidence for God's unity, linking it to 11:18; he also treats the related preceding sentence as a new sentence reinforcing 11:18 and a class who lost themselves, citing 6:12. He identifies the claims as idol intercession and protection from hardship and sees the idols' disappearance as mockery, citing 46:28. Al-Suddi, reported in al-Durr, says those who lost themselves cheated or deprived themselves. Al-Biqa'i explains the immediately preceding inability to thwart as inability to prevent God's will, doubling as increase by an equal or greater amount, and capacity as bodily power. Islahi says invented gods and hoped-for support are useless and leave worshipers without insight. Study Quran says fabricated idols, ideas and beliefs ultimately abandon them, citing 6:24, 6:54, 10:30, 16:87 and 28:75. Al-Samarrai links the judgment to 11:19-21: their obstruction of God's path and misleading of others brought multiplied punishment."}]}

Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī and the Study Quran report the flock or pasture question; al-Bayḍāwī reports alarm and the question about Joseph. The accounts vary in those added actions."}, {"id": "12:16/q09/p2", "position": "After the flock question Jacob collapsed, and Judah checked him for life.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports Judah lamenting that they lost their brother and killed their father with grief."}, {"id": "12:16/q09/p3", "position": "Jacob asked whether some affliction or wage had struck them and then asked where Joseph was.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this wording of the initial question rather than a question about the flock."}, {"id": "12:16/q09/p4", "position": "On hearing Joseph was dead Jacob fainted and remained unconscious until the next morning.", "reasons": "The Study Quran reports that the brothers poured water on him."}]}
{"id": "12:16/q10", "question": "How is yabkūn parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q10/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing the brothers as they came.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās states this directly. Al-Ṭabrisī calls Jacob's crying circumstantial in his parsing. Al-Samīn says it means they came weeping; Bursevī likewise makes it circumstantial and glosses it in Persian as deliberate weeping. Al-Burhān says the present verb in the circumstantial phrase depicts weeping already underway at arrival and renewing moment by moment."}]}
{"id": "12:16/q11", "question": "Were the brothers' tears genuine?", "turns_on": "Whether visible crying represented real remorse over Joseph or a performance supporting the wolf story.", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q11/p1", "position": "Their weeping was staged to make a false account seem true.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim's al-Ḥasan calls them lying sinners. Al-Wāḥidī says they used it to seem innocent of the alleged wolf attack. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say the crying was feigned; Bursevī's Persian gloss calls it deliberate, and his quotation from the Mathnawī says the displayed grief concealed envy and malice. Al-Biqāʿī defines crying as tears flowing in sadness yet says that tears can be feigned. Al-Ālūsī says liars imitate sorrow, and another reported explanation says they hid joy at success in darkness. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says they wept to disguise their plot and gain trust."}, {"id": "12:16/q11/p2", "position": "They may have sincerely regretted harming Joseph while hiding the reason for their grief.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī allows genuine regret, though they blamed a wolf when speaking to Jacob."}]}
{"id": "12:16/q12", "question": "Do tears establish that a person's claim is true?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q12/p1", "position": "Tears do not establish truth, and a judge must decide by the prescribed standard or truth.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports Mujālid from al-Shaʿbī: Shurayḥ answered a crying woman by citing the brothers. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Biqāʿī state the general inference. Al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit al-Aʿmash's warning not to believe a weeper; al-Ālūsī gives his stronger quip that even one's father should not be believed. Al-Qushayrī and the Study Quran report that a complete hypocrite can control tears at will. Al-Ālūsī cites a couplet proposing tears crossing the cheek as a way to distinguish genuine from imitated weeping."}]}
{"id": "12:16/q13", "question": "What spiritual condition is shown by a liar's ability to weep at will?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q13/p1", "position": "It is a sign of divine abandonment or complete hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī calls the enabling of a liar's voluntary tears God's abandonment and reports that fully developed hypocrisy lets a person command his eyes; the Study Quran repeats the hypocrisy report."}]}
{"id": "12:16/q14", "question": "What is omitted in the narrative transition to the brothers' return?", "turns_on": "The two reconstructions supply different unspoken stages of the surrounding story.", "positions": [{"id": "12:16/q14/p1", "position": "Jacob granted the brothers' request and sent Joseph with them.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says this connective clause is omitted because context supplies it."}, {"id": "12:16/q14/p2", "position": "The brothers arrived without Joseph, Jacob asked about him, and they gave their wolf claim.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān supplies this unspoken exchange from the context after their arrival."}]}
